\begin{example} \end{example}[Isometries of Euclidean space]

Source: petersen:page-0028 ↗ def:pet-ch1-isometry-group ↗ def:pet-ch1-riemannian-isometry

1. ch1:1.3.1\[ \operatorname {Iso}(\mathbb {R}^n,g_{\mathrm{eu}}) =\mathbb {R}^n\rtimes O(n) =\{ x\mapsto v+Ox:v\in \mathbb {R}^n,\ O\in O(n)\} , \] with unique $v,O$. For every $p$, the isotropy is isomorphic to $O(n)$ and $\mathbb {R}^n\simeq \operatorname {Iso}/\operatorname {Iso}_p$. More generally, a homogeneous manifold is the quotient of its isometry group by an isotropy subgroup. \end{example}
Proof

↗ ex:pet-ch1-isometry-group-euclidean ↗ rem:pet-ch1-ex-17 ↗ rem:pet-ch1-ex-19 \sketch Affine orthogonal maps are isometries. Conversely, a Riemannian isometry $F$ preserves curve length by item 3. Applying item 3 to the image of the segment from $x$ to $y$ gives $|F(x)-F(y)|\le |x-y|$; applying the same argument to $F^{-1}$ gives equality. Mazur–Ulam then makes $F$ affine: $F(x)=F(0)+Ox$ with $O\in O(n)$.
